scope: integrated research and usability pilot, not complete scholarly validation

claims.statement: The February 1978 discovery of the Coyolxauhqui monolith prompted the Proyecto Templo Mayor excavations.
Eduardo Matos Moctezuma founded the Proyecto Templo Mayor.
The project excavated the main Mexica temple and other structures of the sacred precinct.
Archaeological work has documented enlargements of the Templo Mayor.
The Templo Mayor was dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tláloc.
The 2025 INAH reconstruction exhibition used topographic surveys of excavated architectural remains.
Every construction stage can be identified and dated by a visitor from exposed stone color alone.
An INAH October 2024 report stated that the project had produced more than 1,300 academic publications and 118 theses.
The Templo Mayor has seven identified major construction stages, with additional partial enlargements.
Successive enlargements covered earlier temple structures, producing nested archaeological building phases.
The Templo Mayor had twin upper shrines and a double stairway, a form retained across enlargements.
Workers discovered the Coyolxauhqui monolith on 21 February 1978, initiating archaeological rescue and the Proyecto Templo Mayor.

features.name: Successive temple enlargements
features.visitor_instruction: Find the official site diagram showing the successive construction stages. Compare the outlines and stairways of the nested phases; do not assign dates to an individual wall without its labeled stage.
features.explanation: Archaeologists distinguish successive building campaigns through superimposed architecture, construction interfaces, and excavation context. The common seven-stage framework summarizes major phases, but the dating and identification of individual subphases require specific archaeological documentation.
features.access: Museum or site admission may be required; sightline unverified

features.name: Twin shrines and stairways
features.visitor_instruction: Use the official site plan to locate the paired summit sanctuary arrangement and the stairways that approached it. Check what remains are actually visible from your position.
features.explanation: The main temple was associated with Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. The arrangement and its interpretations must be documented using excavation publications, archaeological finds, and historical accounts rather than assuming every feature can be seen today.
features.visual_needed: Plan of summit and labeled reconstructed elevation

features.name: Coyolxauhqui monolith discovery
features.visitor_instruction: Locate the museum or site interpretation identifying the Coyolxauhqui monolith, then compare the dated discovery photograph with a modern museum image if licensing permits.
features.explanation: The 1978 discovery became a pivotal event in the modern archaeological project. The discovery circumstances, iconographic interpretation, and chronology are separate claims and need separate evidence.
features.visual_needed: Rights-cleared 1978 excavation photograph and object record
features.access: Museum display and current access unverified

features.name: Offerings and excavation context
features.visitor_instruction: Find an object label that identifies an offering number and excavation context. Compare the object-level label with a published excavation report.
features.explanation: An offering is not simply a collection of objects: its position, stratigraphy, association, and recorded deposition are central to interpretation.
features.visual_needed: Published offering plan and catalog image
